body.question: In a 2 mm copper wire carrying 1 ampere, how fast do the electrons drift along the wire?
body.reveal: About 23 micrometres per second, a slow crawl. Yet a lamp lights at once, because a change in current travels as an electromagnetic wave at a significant fraction of the speed of light, far faster than the electrons drift.

probes.question: In a 2 mm copper wire carrying 1 ampere, how fast do the electrons drift along the wire?

claims.claim: Drift speed in 2 mm copper wire at 1 A is about 23 micrometres per second (title, reveal, probe, unit and range)
claims.note: Verified by calculation: v = I/(nAe) = 1/(8.5e28 * 3.14e-6 m2 * 1.602e-19) = 2.34e-5 m/s = about 23 um/s; the page's worked example (copper, 1 A, 2 mm diameter) gives 2.3e-5 m/s. Unit um/s and the 1..1,000,000 log range contain 23.

claims.claim: Electron flow in solids is slow (a slow crawl)
claims.quote: Typically, electric charges in solids flow slowly.

claims.claim: A change in current travels as an electromagnetic wave at very high speed
claims.quote: gives rise to an electromagnetic wave that propagates at very high speed

claims.claim: That wave speed is a significant fraction of the speed of light
claims.quote: This speed is usually a significant fraction of the speed of light

claims.claim: The wave is far faster than the electrons' drift (so a lamp responds at once)
claims.quote: is therefore many times faster than the drift velocity of the electrons
claims.note: 'Lamp lights at once' is the everyday consequence of the very fast wave; the page does not mention lamps.
